notes: C: dash/wall-jump/coyote loop repeats even with juice stripped (documented core-loop design).
C: each chapter (1-7+Core) introduces a new mechanic through to the end.
C: performative+cognitive+emotional challenge types present (e.g. Ch.6 panic sequence).
C: dash/wall-jump fundamentals are prerequisites for later chapter mechanics and advanced tech.
C: deaths are legible to a specific timing/input mistake. M?: floaty jump arc/absorb-dash hitbox looseness sometimes obscures cause of death (mechanical design fact, not review opinion).
C: near-instant retry and visibly cleaner runs make improvement felt in play.
C: chapter-clear screen shows time/deaths. M?: uncertain whether per-stage summary breaks down performance beyond time/score.
C: precision-platformer deaths vs clean dash chains are highly legible to a spectator.
C: dash-refill flash/chapter-clear fanfare attach to the skill-defining dash/wall-jump actions.
M?: uncertain whether some absorbed weapons dominate the weakness chain, reducing others' value.
C: minimal in-loop decisions (route choice) require no pause.
C: speedrun community actively argues route/tech (wavedash vs hyperdash). M?: little evidence of build/route argument culture; smaller, less contentious community.
C: no permadeath/compounding resource loss; a persistent choice can't silently ruin a run.
M?: level paths fairly fixed with only minor execution variation, per typical design.
C: unintended tech (wavedash, hyperdash, demo-dash) discovered and later embraced by devs in Farewell. M?: no strong evidence of a notable sequence-break/glitch culture.
C: strawberries, no-death runs, golden strawberries, B/C-sides are player-set goals.
C: dash+wall-jump+climb-stamina combo is a widely recognized, distinctive movement identity.
C: chapter design deliberately breathes between spikes, guaranteeing both fails and clears en route.
M?: precision-timing calibration considered uneven given documented floaty-jump/hit-detection issues (mechanical, not review-derived).
C: hazards are clearly telegraphed and fair (color-coded spikes, wind-up cues). M?: some enemy attacks/hitboxes documented as inconsistent, reading as illegitimately advantaged.
C: near-zero-cost, near-instant respawn is a headline design feature.
M?: checkpoint spacing in some stages forces replay of already-mastered sections.
C: assist mode + no resource lockouts prevent hopelessness.
C: renowned deterministic, frame-consistent input handling (buffering/coyote time). M?: floaty jump physics and inconsistent absorb-dash hit detection undercut reliable input-outcome mapping.
C: no meaningful randomness in deterministic level design. M: also deterministic action-platforming, no meaningful randomness.
C: pacing (breathing rooms between spikes) keeps demanding-but-not-overwhelming workload, a stated design goal. M?: some segments (e.g. instant-death hazards) may exceed comfortable workload.
C: next room/strawberry is always immediately visible as a reason to continue.
C: chapter ends/checkpoints are clean stopping points.
C: continuation pull is mastery-driven; no random-reward or dark-pattern compulsion loops.
C: devs have documented tuned input buffering/coyote-time for tight response. M?: floaty/delayed-feeling jump and dash is a specifically documented control critique tied to physics tuning.
C: jump/dash always paired with immediate sound+visual.
C: clean, readable animation with minimal obscuring effects.

C: restrained juice never obscures precision-platforming readability, essential to the genre. M?: cutscene spectacle sometimes runs ahead of core-gameplay clarity, though gameplay juice itself is restrained.
C: momentum-based air control/dash arc is deliberately tuned and widely felt as weighty. M?: floaty jump lacking weight/momentum grounding is the most specifically documented physics critique.
C: pure movement (dash/wall-jump) is celebrated as satisfying with no goal at all (movement-tech videos).
C: dash availability shown via hair color; hazards clearly color-coded.
C?: sparse UI means little to inspect on demand; death-count in a menu is the main example.
C: acclaimed dynamic-layered soundtrack (Lena Raine).
C: cohesive pixel-art style, effects match consistently. M?: cel-shaded 3D character models against 2D backgrounds is a documented visual-pipeline mismatch.
M?: voice-line repetitiveness/quality is a specifically documented critique of the voice direction.
C: short (clear room)/medium (chapter, strawberries)/long (summit, B/C-sides) goals run simultaneously.
C?: within a chapter the eventual outcome (reaching the top) is rarely in doubt — uncertainty is more about death count than arc outcome.
C: each chapter's new mechanic changes how the game is played; almost no numeric progression exists at all.
C: chapters deliberately alternate intense challenge rooms with calmer narrative/exploration segments.
C: iconic hard-won moments (Ch.9 Farewell, golden-strawberry runs) are widely and specifically remembered. M?: little evidence of engineered, specifically-remembered triumph moments.
C: new mechanics arrive every chapter through to the end (Core/Ch.7).
M?: collectible/upgrade pacing not well characterized; assumed moderate.
C: unscripted emergent tech (wavedash, hyperdash, demo-dash) from dash+jump+wall interactions, later embraced by devs. M?: little evidence of comparable emergent, unscripted mechanic interactions.
C: large community trades movement-tech discoveries. M?: little evidence of a comparable tech-trading community.
C: assist mode + fair telegraphing gives confidence any challenge is closable with effort.
C: worst case for experimentation is an instant, costless retry — exploration is safe and often reveals tech.
C: hidden crystal hearts, secret rooms, golden strawberries, B/C-sides reward players who go looking. M?: some collectibles/secrets exist but a rich hidden-content culture is not well evidenced.

C: fantasy of a determined climber overcoming struggle is delivered directly through precise athletic movement. M?: heroic-robot fantasy is undercut somewhat by floaty controls working against a 'precise machine' feel.

C: frustration, triumph, anxiety (thematically reinforced), sadness and joy all occur in a normal playthrough. M?: narrative is comparatively shallow; emotional range mostly frustration/satisfaction from action gameplay.
C: Ch.6 'Reflection' is a deliberately dread-filled sequence widely regarded as memorable. M: tonally light sci-fi adventure with no clear deliberate negative-valence peak.
C: being a skilled climber (fantasy) requires literally mastering the climbing mechanics (skill) — tightly bound both ways.
C: widely reported as a game people reflect on after playing, tied to its mental-health themes. M?: niche following; little evidence players report thinking about it outside play.
C: Prologue chapter teaches dash entirely through minimal-text, in-play environmental teaching. M?: relies more on explicit tutorial prompts/text early on, per typical console-action-game convention.
C: Prologue chapter is proportioned exactly to teach the novel dash mechanic, no more.
C: very little menu time; the game is play-dense.

C: rules are consistent and legible; surprises come from creative combination of visible mechanics, not hidden unfairness. M?: inconsistent hit-detection can produce surprises from mechanical looseness rather than fair combination.
C: near-instant respawn, frequent checkpoints, essentially zero loading. M?: checkpoint gaps and slower respawn/loading were a specifically documented friction point.
C: extensive assist mode (game speed, invincibility, infinite stamina, dash assist) broadens access without altering the default S1 experience.

C: hazards are clearly telegraphed (color-coding, wind-up animation) ahead of requiring a response. M?: floaty/inconsistent physics sometimes makes deaths feel untelegraphed relative to design intent.
